newsitem.title: UK: Asia, Latam lead non-OPEC Q1 output growth - survey.
newsitem.headline: Asia, Latam lead non-OPEC Q1 output growth - survey.

text.p: Growth in oil output from the world's main non-OPEC suppliers accelerated in the first quarter of 1997, rising 332,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 39.46 million bpd, a survey by Reuters found.
The increase was led by Latin America and Asia with rises of three and two percent respectively over average output for 1996.

Asia recorded the biggest single volume increase in the first quarter, pumping an extra 116,000 bpd at an average 5.586 million bpd thanks to a jump in Chinese and Australian output which more than compensated for modest falls in India and Malaysia.
China produced 3.249 million bpd in the first three months of the year, up from 3.17 million bpd, as output from offshore fields and in the east of the country gathered pace.

Brazil was the pick of the Latin American non-OPEC producers, its 56,000 bpd increase to 865,000 bpd combining with a smaller rise from Argentina to make up for weaker performances from Colombia and Ecuador.

The survey covers more than 90 percent of the oil pumped by suppliers other than Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) members and includes natural gas liquids, as well as crude, from most countries.
North American output rose to 14.196 million bpd from 14.140 million last year despite a 60,000 bpd fall in U.S. production.
Canada pumped an extra 70,000 bpd at 2.52 million bpd and Mexico added another 46,000 bpd to 3.326 million bpd.
Former Soviet states appeared to have turned the corner, with output rising by 58,000 bpd in the first quarter to 6.683 million bpd on the back of small increases in both Russia and Kazakhstan.
Europe's contribution was flat, however, with a fall in Norwegian output due to bad weather in the North Sea wiping out increases in Denmark and Britain.
Non-OPEC Middle East and African production rose by a modest 18,000 bpd to 3.832 million bpd thanks to rising output in Angola and Congo which cancelled out losses in Egypt.
Figures in millions of barrels per day come mostly from national governments. Other sources include oil companies and the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA):
